The Origin of Consciousness in the Breakdown of the Bicameral Mind by Julian Jaynes

I was attracted to this book when I saw a comment about it from someone who I knew to be pretty damn smart. He said it was either the craziest thing, or the smartest thing, he's ever read. That got me hooked.

The first chapter is terrific. It can be harder to plow through after that, but there's rewards even to skimming and spot-reading the tougher sections.

One of the the things that I encountered here that really made an impact on me is the idea that when you are speaking (or writing, as I am now) that the words pop into your consciousness and we become aware of them pretty much at the same instant as we say them. There is a second mind, mostly invisible to the conscious mind, that feeds us these words. This second mind also does most of the thinking and learning, too. It's pretty much 95% of who you are, and it's invisible to what we call our conscious selves.

The communication between these two minds, and the impact that this may have had on human history, is the topic of the book. He's suggesting the not-entirely-crazy idea that this communication between our two minds evolved fairly recently in our past - say, around 5k or 10k years ago - and is tied to the emergence of writing and language. Before that there may have been a much more primitive mechanism for how our brains worked. Fascinating stuff.
